items.followUp: Define a compound. Differentiate between an atom and a molecule.

rubric.why: Checks the defining idea that an element contains only one kind of atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining an element as a pure substance made up of only one kind of atom.

rubric.why: Checks that a molecule is a neutral group of two or more atoms.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for stating that a molecule is an electrically neutral group of two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds.

accept: group of two or more atoms
rubric.why: Checks that a molecular ion is a group of atoms carrying an overall charge.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for defining a molecular ion as a charged group of two or more atoms; examples may support the definition.

modelAnswer: An element is a pure substance made up of only one kind of atom and cannot be decomposed into simpler substances by chemical means.
A molecule is an electrically neutral group of two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds.
A molecular ion is a charged group of two or more atoms.
Examples of molecular ions are NH4+ and SO4^2-.

items.followUp: What is meant by atomic number? State the rules for filling electrons into shells of an atom.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of electronic configuration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining it as the arrangement or distribution of electrons in the shells of an atom.

rubric.why: Checks the rule for the maximum number of electrons in a shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the maximum number of electrons in a shell is given by 2n².

rubric.why: Checks that electrons fill shells in order, beginning with the innermost shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that shells are filled successively, starting with the innermost shell.

rubric.why: Checks the stated limits for electrons in the outermost and first shells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the outermost shell generally contains no more than 8 electrons and the first shell no more than 2.

modelAnswer: Electronic configuration is the arrangement of electrons in the shells of an atom.
The maximum number of electrons in a shell is given by 2n^2, where n is the shell number.
Electrons fill the shells successively, starting with the innermost shell.
The outermost shell generally contains no more than 8 electrons; the first shell can contain no more than 2.

items.followUp: Explain single and triple covalent bonds, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Checks that a single covalent bond involves sharing one pair of electrons.
rubric.description: Electron sharing in a single covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that one pair of electrons is shared.

rubric.why: Checks the conventional representation of a single covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating or showing that a single covalent bond is represented by one line.

rubric.why: Checks that a double covalent bond involves sharing two pairs of electrons.
rubric.description: Electron sharing in a double covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that two pairs of electrons are shared.

rubric.why: Checks the conventional representation of a double covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating or showing that a double covalent bond is represented by two lines.

rubric.why: Checks the stability gained through sharing electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that sharing electrons helps the atoms attain stable outer shells.

modelAnswer: A single covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one pair of electrons.
It is represented by one line; for example, H—H in a hydrogen molecule.
A double covalent bond is formed when two atoms share two pairs of electrons.
It is represented by two lines; for example, O=O in an oxygen molecule.
In both cases, sharing electrons helps the atoms attain stable outer shells.
